title: String Matching Algorithms
tagline: Finding a pattern inside a text efficiently — from search engines to DNA sequencing, string matching is one of computing's most practical problems.

sections.content:
Every time you press Ctrl+F to find a word in a document, every time a search engine indexes a webpage, every time a virus scanner checks your file against a signature database, and every time a bioinformatics tool hunts a gene sequence through a three-billion-character genome — a **string matching algorithm** is running. The problem sounds deceptively simple: given a **text** T of length n and a **pattern** P of length m, report every position in T where P appears as a substring. But the difference between a naive implementation and a clever one can be the difference between a millisecond and several minutes on large inputs.

The brute-force approach is obvious — slide the pattern along the text one character at a time and compare. This works perfectly for small strings, but its worst-case behaviour is **O(n·m)** comparisons. If you are searching a megabyte of DNA (n ≈ 10⁶) for a hundred-character gene (m = 100), that is up to 100 million character comparisons per query. With a cleverer algorithm, the same search takes at most n + m ≈ 1,000,100 comparisons.

Three classic algorithms cover the entire design space. **Naive (brute-force)** needs no preprocessing and costs O(n·m) worst case — the baseline. **Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP)**, invented in 1977, preprocesses the pattern in O(m) time to build a **failure function** that encodes the pattern's internal repetitions, then scans the text in O(n) — a total of O(n+m), guaranteed worst case with no hash collisions or probabilistic assumptions. **Rabin-Karp**, from 1987, converts the pattern and each sliding window of the text into a **hash value**, comparing hashes in O(1) per window instead of comparing characters one by one — O(n+m) expected time, with a graceful extension to searching for multiple patterns simultaneously.

Understanding these three algorithms builds deep intuition that recurs throughout computer science: the value of **preprocessing**, the power of **amortised analysis**, the trade-off between **worst-case and expected guarantees**, and the engineering art of choosing the right tool for the problem at hand.

sections.title: Three Detectives, One Investigation
sections.content:
Imagine three detectives each searching a thousand-page novel for the phrase 'ABCABD'. Detective Naive reads from page one. At each word, she places the template 'ABCABD' over the text and compares letter by letter. If a mismatch occurs, she slides the template one position to the right and starts the comparison over from scratch — throwing away every clue the previous comparison revealed. She is thorough but wasteful.

Detective KMP prepares differently. Before opening the novel, she studies the pattern itself and notices something: the phrase 'ABCABD' has 'AB' at the start and 'AB' at the end of its prefix 'ABCAB'. This means if she has matched 'ABCAB' but then sees a mismatch at position 5, she does not have to restart from scratch — the 'AB' she just matched at positions 3-4 is the same 'AB' at positions 0-1, so she can resume matching from pattern position 2. She always moves forward through the novel and never re-reads a character she has already seen.

Detective Rabin-Karp works completely differently. She converts the pattern 'ABCABD' into a numeric fingerprint — say, the hash value 42,891. Then she takes each six-letter window of the novel and computes its fingerprint. Most windows produce a different number, so she skips them instantly. Only when a window's fingerprint matches 42,891 does she bother doing a careful character-by-character comparison. She extends naturally to searching for dozens of patterns simultaneously: store all their fingerprints in a lookup table and check whether each window's hash appears in the table in one operation.

sections.title: The Naive Algorithm: Simple and Honest
sections.content:
The naive algorithm is worth understanding precisely because it makes the problem concrete and reveals exactly what the smarter algorithms improve upon.

The outer loop runs from position i = 0 to i = n - m (inclusive) — those are the only positions where the pattern can start and still fit inside the text. At each starting position, the inner loop compares T[i+j] with P[j] for j from 0 to m-1. If all m characters match, we record a hit. If any character mismatches, we break the inner loop and move to i+1.

**Best case**: The first character of the pattern never matches any character in the text — every outer iteration does only one comparison, giving O(n) total. For example, searching for pattern 'XYZ' in a text of all 'A's.

**Worst case**: Every attempt almost succeeds before failing at the last character. Classic adversarial input: text = 'AAAA...A' (n A's) and pattern = 'AA...AB' (m-1 A's followed by B). Every starting position matches m-1 characters before the final B fails. There are roughly n-m+1 ≈ n starting positions, giving O(n·m) total comparisons. A text with n = 100,000 and m = 1,000 would need up to 100 million character comparisons.

**Average case in practice**: For natural language text and patterns, the naive algorithm is often fast because mismatches tend to happen after just a few character comparisons. The O(n·m) worst case requires adversarially constructed inputs. This is why the naive algorithm is often acceptable for interactive text search in editors.

The key wasteful behaviour is that every time we slide to a new starting position, we discard all the comparison work from the previous position. If we matched 'ABCAB' and then failed at 'C' vs 'D', we know the text contains 'ABCAB' starting at position i — but the naive algorithm ignores this knowledge and restarts from zero at position i+1.

sections.title: KMP: The Failure Function Idea
sections.content:
KMP's core insight is that when a mismatch occurs at pattern position j (after successfully matching j characters), the characters T[i-j .. i-1] are already known — they equal P[0 .. j-1]. If P[0 .. j-1] contains a prefix that is also a suffix of itself, we can slide the pattern forward by the difference and resume matching from the end of that overlapping prefix, without re-examining any text characters.

Formally, define the **failure function** `lps[j]` (Longest Proper Prefix which is also Suffix) as: the length of the longest proper prefix of the substring P[0..j] that is also a suffix of P[0..j]. 'Proper' means it cannot be the entire string itself.

Examples:
- P = 'ABAAB': lps = [0, 0, 1, 1, 2]
  - lps[0] = 0 (single character, no proper prefix)
  - lps[1] = 0 ('AB' — 'A' is a prefix but is 'A' a suffix? No, suffix is 'B')
  - lps[2] = 1 ('ABA' — 'A' is both prefix and suffix, length 1)
  - lps[3] = 1 ('ABAA' — 'A' matches, 'AB'/'ABA' do not match suffix 'AA'/'BAA')
  - lps[4] = 2 ('ABAAB' — 'AB' is both prefix and suffix, length 2)

- P = 'ABABCABAB': lps = [0, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
  - lps[7] = 3 means 'ABABCABA' has 'ABA' as both prefix and suffix
  - lps[8] = 4 means 'ABABCABAB' has 'ABAB' as both prefix and suffix

During the search phase, when a mismatch occurs at pattern index j, instead of resetting j to 0, we reset j to `lps[j-1]`. This tells us: 'the last `lps[j-1]` characters of the text that we already matched form the beginning of a potentially valid new match.' The text pointer i is never moved backwards — it only ever advances. This is why the search phase is O(n).

Why is the total work O(n)? The text pointer i increments exactly n times total. The pattern pointer j can decrease when a mismatch occurs, but it can only decrease a total number of times bounded by the total number of times it has increased. Since i increases at most n times and j increases with i, j can decrease at most n times overall. So the total number of operations in the search loop is O(n).

sections.title: KMP: Building the Failure Function
sections.content:
The lps array is itself built by a self-similar process — the pattern is matched against itself using the same sliding idea.

We maintain a pointer `len` representing the length of the current matching prefix-suffix, and a position pointer `i` scanning forward through the pattern starting at index 1 (lps[0] is always 0 by definition).

**Case 1** — P[i] == P[len]: the current character extends the matching prefix-suffix. Set lps[i] = len + 1, then advance both i and len.

**Case 2** — P[i] != P[len] and len > 0: we cannot extend the current prefix-suffix, but we do not give up immediately. We fall back: set len = lps[len-1]. This is the same prefix-suffix trick applied recursively — if 'ABCAB' had a prefix-suffix of length 5, we try the next shorter one. We do NOT increment i; we try again with the shorter prefix.

**Case 3** — P[i] != P[len] and len == 0: there is no prefix-suffix at position i at all. Set lps[i] = 0 and increment i.

The overall time complexity of building lps is O(m): `i` advances at most m times; `len` decreases can only happen as many times as it has increased, and it increases at most m times, so total operations are O(m).

This two-pointer self-matching is a beautiful example of using a problem's structure against itself — the same reasoning that makes the search phase efficient also makes the preprocessing efficient.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The critical detail in the search: after a full match (j === m), we set j = lps[j-1], not j = 0. This allows overlapping matches to be found. For pattern 'AA' in text 'AAAA', lps = [0,1]. After a match at index 0, j resets to lps[1] = 1, meaning we start the next attempt already having matched one 'A' — the second character of the previous match serves as the first character of the next. This yields matches at indices 0, 1, and 2.

sections.title: Rabin-Karp: Turning Strings into Numbers
sections.content:
KMP achieves O(n+m) by being clever about mismatch handling. Rabin-Karp achieves the same expected complexity with a completely different strategy: **avoid character-by-character comparison almost entirely by hashing**.

The central idea: if we had a hash function H such that H(window) == H(pattern) implies window == pattern, we could simply compute hashes and compare integers instead of strings. Comparing two integers is O(1); comparing two strings is O(m). The challenge is computing the hash of each new window quickly as the window slides one position to the right.

**Polynomial rolling hash**: Represent a string s[0..m-1] as a polynomial evaluated at base b, modulo a large prime q:

`H = (s[0] * b^(m-1) + s[1] * b^(m-2) + ... + s[m-1] * b^0) mod q`

When we slide one position right — removing s[0] and adding s[m] — the new hash is:

`H_new = (H_old - s[0] * b^(m-1)) * b + s[m]) mod q`

This is O(1) per slide: subtract the contribution of the character leaving the window (scaled by its position weight `b^(m-1)`), multiply by b to shift all remaining contributions left by one position, then add the new character. We precompute `b^(m-1) mod q` once in O(m), then each slide is O(1).

**Hash collisions**: Two different strings can have the same hash value. A hash match is a **necessary but not sufficient** condition for a real match. So when hashes match, we do a full O(m) character comparison to confirm. If the hash is good, collisions are rare, and the verification step costs nearly nothing amortised. The expected number of false positives when using a prime q ≈ 10^9 is O(n/q) ≈ negligible.

**Multi-pattern advantage**: Rabin-Karp shines when searching for k patterns simultaneously. Precompute all k pattern hashes and store them in a hash set. For each window, compute the rolling hash and check set membership in O(1). A single O(n) pass through the text finds all occurrences of any pattern — whereas running KMP k times would cost O(k·n). This is exactly how antivirus signature databases work: thousands of signatures, one pass through the file.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Algorithm: A Decision Framework
sections.content:
All three algorithms solve the same problem but with different trade-offs. Here is a practical decision framework:

**Use naive search when:**
- The pattern is very short (m ≤ 10) and the text is small. The O(m·n) cost is negligible.
- You want the simplest possible code with no risk of off-by-one errors in the failure function.
- The text comes from natural language and mismatches happen early on average (making the effective complexity much better than O(n·m)).
- You need to ship in five minutes.

**Use KMP when:**
- You need a worst-case guarantee of O(n+m) — for example, when the input might be adversarially constructed (a fuzzer, a competitive programming problem, or a security-critical application).
- You are searching for a single pattern.
- Memory is tight — KMP only needs O(m) extra space for the lps array.
- You want to understand the algorithm that interviewers ask about most frequently for string matching.

**Use Rabin-Karp when:**
- You are searching for **multiple patterns** simultaneously — Rabin-Karp's hash-set approach handles k patterns in one pass instead of k separate passes.
- The pattern is long, making even rare hash collisions cheap relative to the O(m) verification cost.
- You need to detect approximate matches or plagiarism (by comparing hashes of overlapping chunks, a technique used in Dropbox's dedup algorithm and Rsync's delta encoding).
- You can tolerate expected rather than worst-case complexity.

**Beyond these three** — for extremely demanding applications, the **Aho-Corasick** algorithm generalises KMP to multi-pattern search with a guaranteed O(n + total_pattern_length + number_of_matches) complexity. It builds a finite automaton from all patterns and processes the text in a single linear scan. Antivirus engines, network intrusion detection systems, and Grep's `--fixed-strings` mode use variants of this approach when dealing with thousands of patterns.

sections.title: Real-World Applications and Complexity Analysis in Depth
sections.content:
**DNA sequencing**: The human genome has about 3.2 billion base pairs (characters from the alphabet {A, T, C, G}). Finding a gene or a mutation marker (pattern length m = 20–1000 bp) requires O(n) algorithms — naive would be too slow even on modern hardware. BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool), used by every biology lab in the world, uses heuristics built on these ideas.

**Text editors and search tools**: The venerable Unix tool `grep` uses Boyer-Moore-Horspool for single patterns (a different O(n/m) average-case algorithm) and Aho-Corasick for multiple patterns with `-F`. VS Code and Sublime Text use similar algorithms for their Ctrl+F implementations with optional regex engines.

**Network intrusion detection**: Snort and Suricata match network packets against thousands of signatures in real time. Every packet traversing the wire is checked against every signature — a classic multi-pattern problem where Aho-Corasick (built on the same failure-function idea as KMP) is the standard solution.

**Plagiarism detection**: Turnitin and similar tools compute rolling hashes of overlapping k-grams across a document and compare against a database of known texts. This is Rabin-Karp applied at scale.

**Amortised analysis revisited**: The O(n) search bound for KMP is an amortised argument. In any single iteration of the search loop, j might decrease many times before finding a match. But across the entire search, j can decrease at most as many times as it has increased, and it increases at most n times (once per character matched). This 'tokens' argument — assign one token each time j increases, spend one each time it decreases — proves the total work is O(n). Recognising amortised arguments is a key skill for algorithm analysis beyond string matching.

**Space complexity**: Naive needs O(1) extra space. KMP needs O(m) for the lps array. Rabin-Karp needs O(1) extra space beyond storing the hashes. For very large patterns stored in streaming form, Rabin-Karp's O(1) space advantage can matter.

sections.title: Common Mistakes and Edge Cases to Watch
sections.content:
**Off-by-one in naive search**: The outer loop should run `i <= n - m`, not `i < n`. If you use `i < n`, you check starting positions where the pattern cannot possibly fit and risk reading out of bounds.

**Forgetting lps[0] = 0**: The failure function always sets lps[0] = 0 because a single character has no proper prefix. Starting the build loop at i = 1 is correct — start at i = 0 and you immediately cause an off-by-one in the two-pointer logic.

**The fallback chain in buildLPS**: When P[i] != P[len] and len > 0, the correct action is `len = lps[len - 1]`, NOT `len = 0`. Jumping directly to 0 would miss valid shorter prefix-suffixes and produce an incorrect lps table. This is the most common KMP bug.

**Overlapping matches**: After finding a match at position i-j in KMP, the code must set `j = lps[j-1]` to continue searching for the next match. Setting `j = 0` would miss overlapping occurrences. For pattern 'ABA' in text 'ABABA', there are two overlapping matches at indices 0 and 2.

**Negative modulo in Rabin-Karp**: Most languages (Python is an exception) allow `%` to return negative values when the left operand is negative. When removing the leftmost character's contribution, the subtraction can underflow. Always add MOD before taking `% MOD`: `(hash - contribution + MOD) % MOD`.

**Hash collisions producing false positives**: Rabin-Karp must always verify a hash match with direct character comparison. Skipping verification (treating a hash match as a guaranteed string match) is a correctness bug that can silently return wrong results or be exploited for denial-of-service attacks (by crafting inputs that cause many collisions).

**Empty pattern**: Both KMP and Rabin-Karp should handle m = 0 as a special case. An empty pattern technically matches at every position, but most implementations return either an empty list or [0] — clarify the expected behaviour before implementing.

sections.content: **Historical context**: The naive algorithm predates formalism — it was the obvious approach from the earliest days of computing. The Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm was discovered independently by three researchers: James H. Morris first found it, Donald Knuth proved its O(n) complexity, and Vaughan Pratt improved the practical implementation. Their 1977 paper is one of the most-cited in algorithm literature. Rabin-Karp, published in 1987 by Michael O. Rabin and Richard M. Karp, emerged partly from the field of randomised algorithms — its expected-case analysis introduced many computer scientists to probabilistic reasoning about algorithms. The failure function concept in KMP directly inspired the Aho-Corasick automaton (1975), which generalises to multi-pattern matching and is the backbone of modern text search infrastructure.

**Interview insights and exam traps**: KMP is the canonical O(n+m) string matching answer that interviewers expect. The most common follow-up is 'explain the failure function' — practice the definition out loud: 'lps[j] is the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..j] that is also a suffix.' Then trace through a small example like 'ABABC': lps = [0,0,1,2,0]. The second most common trap: 'does i ever go backward in KMP?' — the answer is emphatically no, and that is the core reason the search phase is O(n). For Rabin-Karp, always mention hash collisions and the need for verification — forgetting this suggests you do not understand why the algorithm is probabilistic. For multi-pattern problems, immediately suggest Rabin-Karp (hash set of pattern hashes) or mention Aho-Corasick — this signals advanced knowledge. Finally: naive search is not wrong — for small patterns on natural text it is often faster in practice than KMP due to lower constant factors and cache friendliness.

items: **Naive string matching** slides the pattern across every position in O(n·m) worst case — simple and sufficient for small or average-case inputs but catastrophically slow on adversarial inputs like 'AAAA…' text with 'AAA…B' pattern.

**KMP** preprocesses the pattern into the **lps (failure function) array** in O(m) time by encoding, at each position j, the length of the longest proper prefix of P[0..j] that is also a suffix. During search, mismatches at position j cause j to reset to lps[j-1] rather than 0, reusing already-matched characters without retreating the text pointer i.

**The text pointer i in KMP never moves backward.** This is the key guarantee: i advances at most n times, so the search phase is O(n). The lps fallback chain only moves j — and j can decrease at most as many times as it has increased, giving an O(n) amortised bound for j's total movement.

**Rabin-Karp** uses a **polynomial rolling hash** to represent each m-length window as an integer. Sliding one position costs O(1) by subtracting the outgoing character's contribution and adding the incoming one. Hash matches trigger O(m) verification to handle collisions — expected total O(n+m), worst case O(n·m) with adversarial hash collisions.

**Rabin-Karp excels at multi-pattern search**: precompute all k pattern hashes into a hash set, then one O(n) text scan checks every window against all k patterns simultaneously — far better than k separate O(n) KMP passes.

**Common bugs**: forgetting `+ MOD` before `% MOD` in Rabin-Karp subtraction; using `len = 0` instead of `len = lps[len-1]` in KMP's lps builder; setting j = 0 after a KMP match (misses overlapping occurrences — always use `j = lps[j-1]`); bounding the naive outer loop at n-m rather than n.

**Production reality**: grep uses Boyer-Moore-Horspool (O(n/m) average case, sub-linear!); antivirus tools use Aho-Corasick for thousands of patterns; bioinformatics tools like BLAST hash k-mers for seed-and-extend matching. KMP and Rabin-Karp are the conceptual foundations upon which all of these build.

quiz.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of the naive string matching algorithm on a text of length n and pattern of length m?
options: O(n + m)
O(n log m)
O(n * m)
O(m²)
quiz.explanation: The naive algorithm tries all n−m+1 starting positions and does up to m comparisons at each. The adversarial case is text='AAAA...A' and pattern='AAA...AB': m-1 characters match at every position before failing. This gives (n-m+1)·m ≈ O(n·m) total comparisons.

quiz.question: What does lps[j] store in the KMP failure function (lps = Longest Proper Prefix which is also Suffix)?
options: The position of the last mismatch in pattern[0..j]
The length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..j] that is also a suffix of pattern[0..j]
The number of characters matched so far when processing position j
The index in the text where the pattern last failed to match
quiz.explanation: lps[j] is the length of the longest proper prefix of the substring pattern[0..j] that is simultaneously a suffix of the same substring. 'Proper' means it cannot be the entire string. This value tells KMP where to resume matching after a mismatch at position j+1: reset j to lps[j] and continue without retreating the text pointer.

quiz.question: For pattern 'ABAAB', what is lps[4] (0-indexed)?
quiz.explanation: Pattern[0..4] = 'ABAAB'. Check proper prefixes as potential suffixes: 'A' (len 1) — does 'ABAAB' end in 'A'? No, it ends in 'B'. 'AB' (len 2) — does 'ABAAB' end in 'AB'? Yes! 'ABA' (len 3) — does 'ABAAB' end in 'ABA'? No (ends in 'AAB'). So the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix is 'AB', length 2. lps[4] = 2.

quiz.question: In the KMP search phase, when a mismatch occurs at pattern position j (and j > 0), what happens to the text pointer i?
options: i is reset to the position where the current match attempt started
i stays unchanged — it never moves backward
i is decremented by j to restart from the failed position
i skips forward by m positions to the next candidate
quiz.explanation: The text pointer i in KMP never moves backward — it only ever advances. When a mismatch occurs at pattern position j, only j is updated (set to lps[j-1]). The text pointer i stays where it is. This is the core reason the search phase is O(n): i moves forward exactly n times total across the entire search, giving a linear bound.

quiz.question: After KMP finds a full match ending at text position i, it sets j = lps[j-1] rather than j = 0. Why?
options: To avoid computing lps again from scratch for the next search
To correctly find overlapping matches by reusing the prefix already known to match
To reset i back to the correct starting position of the next search
To handle the case where the pattern is longer than the remaining text
quiz.explanation: Setting j = lps[j-1] after a match reuses the fact that the last lps[j-1] characters of the just-found match also form a valid prefix of the pattern. This allows KMP to find overlapping occurrences. For example, pattern 'ABA' in text 'ABABA': after the match at index 0, j resets to lps[2]=1 (not 0), so the 'A' at index 2 is already counted as the start of the next match, correctly finding a match at index 2.

quiz.question: How does Rabin-Karp update the window hash when sliding one position to the right?
options: Recompute the hash of the new m-character window from scratch — O(m) per slide
Remove the leftmost character's contribution scaled by BASE^(m-1), multiply by BASE, add the new rightmost character — O(1) per slide
XOR the old hash with the removed character and the new character
Multiply the hash by a fixed constant and take modulo — O(1) but loses positional information
quiz.explanation: The rolling hash formula is: new_hash = ((old_hash - s[0] * BASE^(m-1)) * BASE + s[m]) mod q. Removing s[0]'s contribution requires scaling by BASE^(m-1) (its positional weight), then multiplying the remaining sum by BASE (shifts all other characters' weights left by one), then adding the new rightmost character. This is O(1) per slide after a one-time O(m) precomputation of BASE^(m-1).

quiz.question: Why does Rabin-Karp perform a full character-by-character comparison when hashes match?
options: To compute the next rolling hash value more efficiently
Because hash functions can map different strings to the same value — a hash match is necessary but not sufficient for a true match
Character comparison is faster than arithmetic operations for short patterns
To update the lps failure function for subsequent searches
quiz.explanation: Hash collisions occur when two different strings produce the same hash value. A hash match means the strings might be equal, but not certainly. The O(m) character verification step confirms true matches and rejects false positives. With a good hash function and large prime modulus, collisions are rare, so the amortised cost of verification is negligible. Skipping this step would produce incorrect results.

quiz.question: You must search a text for any occurrence of 500 different fixed-length patterns in a single pass. Which approach is most efficient?
options: Run KMP 500 times, once per pattern — O(500 * n) total
Run the naive algorithm 500 times — simplest to implement
Rabin-Karp: precompute all 500 pattern hashes into a hash set, then one O(n) pass checks each window against the set in O(1)
Binary search through a sorted list of patterns at each text position — O(n log 500)
quiz.explanation: Rabin-Karp naturally extends to multi-pattern search: compute all 500 pattern hashes and store them in a hash set (O(500*m) preprocessing). A single O(n) pass through the text computes a rolling hash for each window and checks set membership in O(1) per window. Total: O(n + 500*m) — one pass finds all 500 patterns simultaneously. Running KMP 500 times costs O(500*n), which is 500 times worse.

quiz.question: In the KMP lps-building algorithm, when P[i] != P[len] and len > 0, the correct action is len = lps[len-1]. What goes wrong if you use len = 0 instead?
options: The loop runs forever because i never increments
Valid shorter prefix-suffix matches are missed, producing an incorrect lps array that causes KMP to skip real matches
The algorithm becomes O(m^2) instead of O(m)
lps[0] gets overwritten with an incorrect value
quiz.explanation: When len > 0 and a mismatch occurs, there may be a shorter prefix-suffix that still holds. For example, if len=4 and P[i] != P[4], maybe len=2 still works (lps[3] might be 2). Setting len=0 immediately discards this possibility and may produce lps values that are too small. A wrong lps table causes KMP to either miss valid matches or perform more comparisons than necessary. The fallback chain len = lps[len-1] correctly tries all shorter prefix-suffix lengths.

quiz.question: Text = 'AAAA', Pattern = 'AA'. How many matches does KMP find, and at what indices?
options: 1 match at index 0 only
2 matches at indices 0 and 2
3 matches at indices 0, 1, and 2
4 matches at indices 0, 1, 2, and 3
quiz.explanation: Pattern 'AA' has lps = [0, 1]. Valid starting positions: 0, 1, 2 (n-m = 4-2 = 2). Text[0..1]='AA' matches at index 0. After the match, j = lps[1] = 1 (not 0), so we start the next attempt with 'A' already matched. Text[2]='A' matches P[1]='A', giving a match at index 1. Similarly, a match at index 2. So 3 matches at indices 0, 1, 2. Setting j=0 after each match would only find 2 non-overlapping matches and miss index 1.
